claim: Stress exerts detrimental effects by enhancing fear and impairing its extinction.
source: Stress is known to exert its detrimental effects not only by enhancing fear, but also by impairing its extinction.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract, drawing from prior research consensus.

claim: In earlier studies, stress exposure preceded both fear conditioning and extinction processes.
source: However, in earlier studies stress exposure preceded both processes.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the design of previous studies, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: When fear memories were formed before stress exposure, recall of fear extinction was unaffected.
source: Strikingly, when fear memories were formed before stress exposure, thereby allowing animals to initiate extinction from comparable levels of fear, recall of fear extinction was unaffected.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 1b.

claim: There was a persistent increase in theta activity in the BLA despite unaffected extinction recall.
source: Despite this, we observed a persistent increase in theta activity in the BLA.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Theta activity in the mPFC was normal after stress when fear memories were formed before stress.
source: Theta activity in the mPFC, by contrast, was normal.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 2f.

claim: Stress disrupted mPFC-BLA theta-frequency synchrony.
source: Stress also disrupted mPFC-BLA theta-frequency synchrony and directional coupling.
evidence: This is supported by coherence and amplitude correlation analyses shown in Figure 3.

claim: Stress disrupted directional coupling between mPFC and BLA.
source: Stress also disrupted mPFC-BLA theta-frequency synchrony and directional coupling.
evidence: This is supported by amplitude cross-correlation data in Figure 3c.

claim: In the absence of fear-enhancing effects of stress, fear expression during and after extinction reflects normal regulation of theta activity in the mPFC, not theta hyperactivity in the amygdala.
source: Thus, in the absence of the fear-enhancing effects of stress, the expression of fear during and after extinction reflects normal regulation of theta activity in the mPFC, not theta hyperactivity in the amygdala.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined behavioral and electrophysiological data presented in Figures 1-3.

claim: Repeated stress causes loss of dendrites and spines in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC).
source: For instance, repeated stress causes loss of dendrites and spines in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) (Shansky and Morrison, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shansky and Morrison, 2009.

claim: Chronic stress strengthens the structural basis of synaptic connectivity in the BLA through dendritic growth and spinogenesis.
source: In the basolateral amygdala (BLA), by contrast, chronic stress strengthens the structural basis of synaptic connectivity through dendritic growth and spinogenesis (Chattarji et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chattarji et al., 2015.

claim: Various facets of fear memory expression depend on both the BLA and mPFC.
source: One such behavior involves the expression of fear memories, various facets of which depend on both the BLA and mPFC (Sierra-Mercado et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sierra-Mercado et al., 2011.

claim: Repeated stress has been shown to enhance fear memories and impair their extinction.
source: Repeated stress has been shown to enhance fear memories, as well as impair their extinction (Miracle et al., 2006; Suvrathan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miracle et al., 2006 and Suvrathan et al., 2014.

claim: Previous studies first exposed animals to stress, then subjected them to fear conditioning followed by extinction.
source: These studies, however, first exposed animals to stress, and then subjected them to fear conditioning followed by extinction (Izquierdo et al., 2006; Miracle et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the design of previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: In a majority of studies, stress did not necessarily lead to higher freezing levels during fear recall.
source: In a majority of these studies, stress did not necessarily lead to higher freezing levels during fear recall.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Even though expression of fear was not elevated by prior exposure to stress, it was resistant to subsequent extinction in stressed animals.
source: Even though expression of fear was not elevated by prior exposure to stress, it was resistant to subsequent extinction in stressed animals (Noble et al., 2017; Zhang and Rosenkranz, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Noble et al., 2017 and Zhang and Rosenkranz, 2013.

claim: In a few studies, prior exposure to stress led to stronger fear memories manifested as higher levels of freezing in stressed animals at the beginning of extinction training.
source: In a few studies, however, the behavioral data suggest that prior exposure to stress may have also led to stronger fear memories manifested as higher levels of freezing in stressed animals at the beginning of extinction training (Chauveau et al., 2012; Hoffman et al., 2014; Miracle et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chauveau et al., 2012; Hoffman et al., 2014; and Miracle et al., 2006.

claim: Rats exhibited significantly higher freezing behavior in response to the tone conditioned stimulus (CS) after auditory fear conditioning.
source: Rats were first subjected to auditory fear conditioning (Day 0, Figure 1) at the end of which they exhibited significantly higher freezing behavior in response to the tone conditioned stimulus (CS) (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: 24 hr after the end of chronic stress there was no difference in CS-induced freezing behavior between stressed and unstressed groups.
source: 24 hr after the end of chronic stress there was no difference in CS-induced freezing behavior between the two groups (Day 11, Block1, Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The recall of fear memory formed earlier was not affected by subsequent stress.
source: Thus, the recall of fear memory formed earlier was not affected by subsequent stress.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data in Figure 1b.

claim: Both stressed and unstressed animals were at the same levels of freezing when the extinction protocol was initiated after stress.
source: This ensured that both stressed and unstressed animals were at the same levels of freezing when the extinction protocol was initiated after stress.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data showing no difference in freezing at the start of extinction.

claim: Repeated tone presentations reduced freezing levels significantly such that both groups eventually underwent comparable extinction of fear.
source: Next, repeated tone presentations reduced freezing levels significantly such that both groups eventually underwent comparable extinction of fear, though the stressed rats were slower in achieving the same reduction in freezing (Day 11, Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Stressed rats were slower in achieving the same reduction in freezing during extinction.
source: Next, repeated tone presentations reduced freezing levels significantly such that both groups eventually underwent comparable extinction of fear, though the stressed rats were slower in achieving the same reduction in freezing (Day 11, Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: A day later stressed animals showed no difference in recall of extinction memory compared to unstressed animals.
source: Notably, a day later stressed animals showed no difference in recall of extinction memory compared to unstressed animals (Day 12, Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Freezing levels during both fear and extinction recall were unaffected in stressed animals when fear memories were formed before stress.
source: Thus, freezing levels during both fear and extinction recall were unaffected in stressed animals.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the behavioral data in Figure 1b.

claim: This result differs from past reports of stress-induced deficits in fear extinction.
source: This result differs from past reports of stress-induced deficits in fear extinction.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: Earlier studies subjected animals to fear conditioning and extinction after exposure to stress.
source: However, as mentioned earlier, those earlier studies subjected animals to fear conditioning and extinction after exposure to stress (Izquierdo et al., 2006; Maren and Holmes, 2016; Miracle et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Izquierdo et al., 2006; Maren and Holmes, 2016; and Miracle et al., 2006.

claim: The timing of stress may be a critical determinant of whether extinction recall is impaired.
source: Taken together, this suggests that the timing of stress may be a critical determinant of whether extinction recall is impaired.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the current results with previous studies.

claim: Prior exposure to chronic stress caused a significant impairment in the recall of fear extinction when fear conditioning occurred after stress.
source: Consistent with earlier findings, prior exposure to chronic stress caused a significant impairment in the recall of fear extinction (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Extinction recall was intact in stressed animals when they were subjected to conditioning before chronic stress.
source: This too yielded the same results as seen in the implanted animals – extinction recall was intact in stressed animals (Figure 1d,f) when they were subjected to conditioning before chronic stress.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1d,f.

claim: During fear recall, AEP amplitudes were enhanced in both stressed and unstressed animals.
source: During fear recall, AEP amplitudes (Rogan et al., 1997) were enhanced in both stressed and unstressed animals (Figure 2c,e).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2c,e.

claim: The increase in AEP amplitude was reversed in unstressed animals during extinction recall.
source: However, while this increase was reversed in unstressed animals, it persisted in stressed rats even during extinction recall (Figure 2c,e).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2c,e.

claim: The increase in AEP amplitude persisted in stressed rats even during extinction recall.
source: However, while this increase was reversed in unstressed animals, it persisted in stressed rats even during extinction recall (Figure 2c,e).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2c,e.

claim: Increase in CS-evoked theta power is a neural correlate of conditioned fear.
source: Previous work also identified increase in CS-evoked theta power as a neural correlate of conditioned fear (Likhtik et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Likhtik et al., 2014.

claim: BLA theta power in unstressed animals paralleled the increase, followed by decrease, in freezing during fear and extinction recall respectively.
source: We found BLA theta power (measured as the power of auditory evoked responses in the 2–12 Hz frequency band) in unstressed animals also paralleled the increase, followed by decrease, in freezing during fear and extinction recall respectively (Figure 2d–e).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2d-e.

claim: BLA theta power remained high in stressed animals during extinction recall.
source: By contrast, BLA theta power remained high in stressed animals (Figure 2d–e).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2d-e.

claim: Despite stress-induced theta hyperactivity in the BLA, fear expression was not enhanced during extinction recall.
source: Thus, despite stress-induced theta hyperactivity in the BLA, fear expression was not enhanced during extinction recall.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from combining behavioral and electrophysiological data.

claim: The dmPFC plays an important role in fear expression.
source: To probe this further, we also analyzed the same LFP parameters in the dmPFC, which according to recent studies plays an important role in fear expression (Karalis et al., 2016; Likhtik et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Karalis et al., 2016 and Likhtik et al., 2014.

claim: In the dmPFC of unstressed rats, AEP amplitude increased during fear recall, and this was reversed during extinction recall.
source: In the dmPFC of unstressed rats, AEP amplitude increased during fear recall, and this was reversed during extinction recall (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Stressed animals did not exhibit any change in dmPFC AEP amplitudes during either fear or extinction recall.
source: Stressed animals, however, did not exhibit any change in dmPFC AEP amplitudes during either fear or extinction recall.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Fear conditioning enhanced dmPFC theta power in both stress and unstressed animals.
source: Further, fear conditioning enhanced dmPFC theta power in both stress and unstressed animals (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The enhancement in dmPFC theta power was reversed in both groups during extinction recall.
source: Interestingly, this was reversed in both groups during extinction recall.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Changes in theta power in the dmPFC, during fear and extinction recall, were not affected by stress.
source: In other words, unlike the BLA, changes in theta power in the dmPFC, during fear and extinction recall, were not affected by stress.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological data in Figure 2f.

claim: In stressed animals, bidirectional modulation of theta power in the dmPFC, but not the BLA, accurately mirrored the changes in freezing.
source: Moreover, in stressed animals, bidirectional modulation of theta power in the dmPFC, but not the BLA, accurately mirrored the changes in freezing, a behavioral expression of fear.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing behavioral and electrophysiological data.

claim: The gradual decrease in dmPFC theta power paralleled the significant within-session reduction in freezing during the acquisition of extinction in both control and stressed animals.
source: Interestingly, the gradual decrease in dmPFC theta power paralleled the significant within-session reduction in freezing during the acquisition of extinction (Day 11, Figure 1b) in both control and stressed animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b,d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b,d.

claim: There was no difference in the time course of reduction in dmPFC theta power between stressed versus control animals during extinction.
source: However, unlike the slower time course of extinction in the stressed rats, there was no difference in the time course of reduction in dmPFC theta power between stressed versus control animals.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Analysis of BLA theta power during extinction learning did not reveal any significant differences that paralleled the gradual within-session decrease in freezing levels.
source: Similar analysis of BLA theta power during extinction learning (Day 12, Figure 1b) did not reveal any significant differences that paralleled the gradual within-session decrease in freezing levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b,c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b,c.

claim: Theta frequency oscillations synchronize dmPFC–BLA circuits during expression of fear behavior.
source: Thus, in light of recent reports that theta frequency oscillations synchronize dmPFC–BLA circuits during expression of fear behavior (Karalis et al., 2016; Likhtik et al., 2014), we investigated whether the tone-evoked increases in theta power (Figure 2) were accompanied by enhanced theta-frequency synchrony between the two areas, and if this was in anyway affected by stress.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Karalis et al., 2016 and Likhtik et al., 2014.

claim: In unstressed rats, the CS elicited significantly higher theta coherence during fear recall.
source: In unstressed rats, consistent with earlier reports, the CS elicited significantly higher theta coherence during fear recall (Likhtik et al., 2014), and this increase persisted during extinction recall as well (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by coherence data shown in Figure 3b and citation to Likhtik et al., 2014.

claim: The increase in theta coherence persisted during extinction recall in unstressed rats.
source: In unstressed rats, consistent with earlier reports, the CS elicited significantly higher theta coherence during fear recall (Likhtik et al., 2014), and this increase persisted during extinction recall as well (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by coherence data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: In stressed animals, there was no change in BLA-dmPFC theta-frequency coherence.
source: Notably, in stressed animals, there was no change in BLA-dmPFC theta-frequency coherence (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by coherence data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Stress appears to completely suppress the dynamic, behaviorally relevant enhancement in BLA-dmPFC coherence that is seen during both fear and extinction recall in unstressed animals.
source: Thus, stress appears to completely suppress the dynamic, behaviorally relevant enhancement in BLA-dmPFC coherence that is seen during both fear and extinction recall in unstressed animals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the coherence data in Figure 3b.

claim: Theta activity in the dmPFC leads that in the BLA during recall of both fear and extinction memories in unstressed rats.
source: This reveals that theta activity in the dmPFC leads that in the BLA during recall of both fear and extinction memories in unstressed rats (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by amplitude cross-correlation data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The dmPFC-to-BLA directional influence is absent in stressed animals.
source: However, this dmPFC-to-BLA directional influence is absent in stressed animals.
evidence: This is supported by amplitude cross-correlation data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Chronic stress causes a decoupling of activity between the dmPFC and BLA, as evidenced by a complete disruption of the increase in dmPFC-BLA theta synchrony and dmPFC-to-BLA directional influence.
source: Together, these data suggest that chronic stress causes a decoupling of activity between the two brain areas, as evidenced by a complete disruption of the increase in dmPFC-BLA theta synchrony and dmPFC-to-BLA directional influence normally seen during the recall of fear and extinction memories.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the coherence and directional coupling data in Figure 3.

claim: This decoupling is evident across all trial blocks during the acquisition of extinction.
source: This decoupling is also evident across all trial blocks during the acquisition of extinction the previous day (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The breakdown in mPFC-BLA theta-frequency synchrony and directional coupling could be one reason why enhanced BLA theta activity was not manifested as higher freezing in stressed animals.
source: This breakdown in mPFC-BLA theta-frequency synchrony and directional coupling could be one reason why enhanced BLA theta activity was not manifested as higher freezing in stressed animals.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the combined behavioral and electrophysiological data.

claim: When stressed animals started extinguishing fear memories from the same level of freezing as their unstressed counterparts, their ability to recall extinction memory remained intact.
source: The present study, specifically designed to administer chronic stress after the formation of fear memory, reveals that when stressed animals started extinguishing fear memories from the same level of freezing as their unstressed counterparts, their ability to recall extinction memory remained intact.
evidence: This is a summary of the main behavioral finding supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Stressed animals exhibited a deficit in extinction recall when faced with the challenge of extinguishing fear memories strengthened by prior exposure to stress.
source: This is in contrast to past findings wherein stressed animals exhibited a deficit in extinction recall when faced with the challenge of extinguishing fear memories strengthened by prior exposure to stress.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: Repeated immobilization stress (4 h/day for 14 days) administered after auditory fear conditioning did not affect the expression of previously acquired fear memories.
source: This is consistent with earlier findings that repeated immobilization stress (4 h/day for 14 days) administered after auditory fear conditioning did not affect the expression of previously acquired fear memories (Meyer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Meyer et al., 2014.

claim: The same immobilization stress, when administered before fear conditioning, elicited a robust increase in fear recall.
source: However, the same immobilization stress, when administered before fear conditioning, elicited a robust increase in fear recall.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Meyer et al., 2014 (implied from context).

claim: The timing of chronic stress exposure, with respect to fear conditioning, is a key determinant of how subsequent extinction of fear is affected by stress.
source: Together, these results suggest that the timing of chronic stress exposure, with respect to fear conditioning, is a key determinant of how subsequent extinction of fear is affected by stress.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the current results with previous studies.

claim: Stress acts primarily on acquisition, and the earlier findings from pre-conditioning stress experiments were not the result of a deficit in fear extinction per se.
source: This dissociation of the effects of stress on acquisition versus extinction of fear conditioning suggests that stress acts primarily on acquisition, and the earlier findings from pre-conditioning stress experiments were not the result of a deficit in fear extinction per se.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current findings and comparison with previous studies.

claim: Deficient fear extinction was only observed in previously stressed adolescent, but not adult, rats.
source: For instance, deficient fear extinction was only observed in previously stressed adolescent, but not adult, rats (Zhang and Rosenkranz, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang and Rosenkranz, 2013.

claim: Despite no visible behavioral effect of stress on fear expression, in vivo recordings reveal a robust impact of stress on amygdalar activity, as evidenced by enhanced theta activity in the BLA that failed to reverse even after the animals exhibited normal extinction recall.
source: Interestingly, despite no visible behavioral effect of stress on fear expression, our in vivo recordings reveal a robust impact of stress on amygdalar activity, as evidenced by enhanced theta activity in the BLA that failed to reverse even after the animals exhibited normal extinction recall (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Enhanced theta activity in the BLA after stress is consistent with earlier findings on physiological and structural strengthening of excitatory synaptic connectivity, as well as reduced inhibitory tone, in the BLA after stress.
source: This is consistent with earlier findings on physiological and structural strengthening of excitatory synaptic connectivity, as well as reduced inhibitory tone, in the BLA after stress (Suvrathan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Suvrathan et al., 2014.

claim: These changes point to possible synaptic mechanisms in the BLA for the stress-induced strengthening of subsequent encoding of fear memories.
source: Together, these changes point to possible synaptic mechanisms in the BLA for the stress-induced strengthening of subsequent encoding of fear memories.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the current findings and previous literature.

claim: Chronic stress did not disrupt normal bidirectional modulation of mPFC theta activity, which in turn was reflected in normal freezing behavior during recall of fear and extinction.
source: The same chronic stress, on the other hand, did not disrupt normal bidirectional modulation of mPFC theta activity, which in turn was reflected in normal freezing behavior during recall of fear and extinction (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: There are strong correlations between mPFC theta-frequency oscillations and conditioning-induced freezing behavior.
source: For instance, recent work has demonstrated strong correlations between mPFC theta-frequency oscillations and conditioning-induced freezing behavior (Likhtik et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Likhtik et al., 2014.

claim: Normal mPFC theta activity is decoupled from theta hyperactivity in the BLA, possibly reducing the latter's influence on fear expression.
source: Furthermore, we find normal mPFC theta activity to be decoupled from theta hyperactivity in the BLA, possibly reducing the latter's influence on fear expression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the coherence and directional coupling data.

claim: A single episode of stress can weaken functional connectivity between the mPFC and BLA measured by resting state fMRI.
source: This is similar to a report that even a single episode of stress can weaken functional connectivity between the two areas measured by resting state fMRI (Liang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liang et al., 2014.

claim: Stress-induced disruptions in prefrontal-to-amygdala connectivity affect social interaction and anxiety-related behaviors in rodents.
source: Indeed, such stress-induced disruptions in prefrontal-to-amygdala connectivity is also known to affect social interaction and anxiety-related behaviors in rodents (Adhikari et al., 2015; Hultman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Adhikari et al., 2015 and Hultman et al., 2016.

claim: The regulation of remote fear memories by stress (i.e. pre-stress conditioning) is different from that of more recent fear memories (i.e. post-stress conditioning).
source: Specifically, these findings suggest that the regulation of remote fear memories by stress (i.e. pre-stress conditioning, Figure 4b) is different from that of more recent fear memories (i.e. post-stress conditioning, Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined behavioral and electrophysiological findings.

claim: Neural circuits mediating the recall of fear memories shifts over time.
source: While stress-induced disruption in mPFC-BLA directional coupling and theta-frequency synchrony (Figure 3) may explain why enhanced BLA theta activity did not result in stress-induced enhancement in freezing, another intriguing possibility arises from a recent report that neural circuits mediating the recall of fear memories shifts over time (Do-Monte et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Do-Monte et al., 2015.

claim: Optogenetic silencing of BLA reduced freezing when it was performed 6 hr, but not 7 days, after auditory fear conditioning.
source: Specifically, this study showed that optogenetic silencing of BLA reduced freezing when it was performed 6 hr, but not 7 days, after auditory fear conditioning.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Do-Monte et al., 2015 (implied from context).

claim: The post-conditioning stress protocol may have outlasted BLA involvement in expression of fear and could explain why enhanced BLA excitability was no longer reflected in freezing at that remote time point.
source: Since our post-conditioning stress protocol was carried out for 10 days, it may have outlasted BLA involvement in expression of fear and could also explain why enhanced BLA excitability was no longer reflected in freezing at that remote time point (Day 11; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the current findings and the Do-Monte et al. study.

claim: In vivo inactivation of the BLA had no impact on fear expression 10 days after fear conditioning in either stressed or control rats.
source: Strikingly, this targeted inactivation of the BLA had no impact on fear expression at this time point in either stressed or control rats (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Freezing levels in the muscimol-infused control and stressed rats did not differ from the freezing levels seen in stressed/control animals that did not receive any infusions in earlier experiments.
source: Further, freezing levels in the muscimol-infused control and stressed rats did not differ from the freezing levels seen in stressed/control animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c) that did not receive any infusions in earlier experiments (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c and Figure 1f.

claim: Fear memories formed 10 days ago no longer depend on BLA activity in either control or stressed animals.
source: Thus, we found that in vivo inactivation of the BLA no longer affects the recall of fear memories that were formed before the 10 day stress exposure. While more detailed analyses will be required to test all aspects of this model, these preliminary results suggest that fear memories formed 10 days ago no longer depend on BLA activity in either control or stressed animals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the muscimol inactivation experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: When fear memories were formed after exposure to chronic stress, stressed animals show enhanced freezing during both acquisition and recall of extinction memory.
source: On the other hand, when fear memories were formed after exposure to the same chronic stress, the behavioural effects on freezing are very different, as has also been reported in earlier studies that employed a post-stress conditioning strategy (Maren and Holmes, 2016; Miracle et al., 2006; Rau and Fanselow, 2009). Animals that were fear conditioned after stress show enhanced freezing during both acquisition and recall of extinction memory.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data in Figure 1e and citations to previous studies.

claim: Stressed animals will recall and extinguish fear memories that were formed only 1 day ago when fear conditioning occurs after stress.
source: For instance, in contrast to the pre-stress conditioning situation, stressed animals will recall and extinguish fear memories that were formed only 1 day ago.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental design shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Stress-induced BLA hyperactivity will be manifested as stronger fear memories that are resistant to subsequent extinction when fear conditioning occurs after stress.
source: As a result, stress-induced BLA hyperactivity will be manifested as stronger fear memories that are resistant to subsequent extinction (as evidenced by higher freezing during extinction recall in CIS rats, Figure 1e).
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the current findings and previous literature.

claim: It is the sustained enhancement in BLA theta activity, not normal regulation of dmPFC activity, that is likely to drive higher freezing in stressed rats during extinction learning and extinction recall when fear conditioning occurs after stress.
source: Thus, now it is the sustained enhancement in BLA theta activity, not normal regulation of dmPFC activity, that is likely to drive higher freezing in stressed rats during extinction learning and extinction recall (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the current findings.

claim: The disruption of mPFC-BLA theta-frequency coherence and directional coupling is likely to impair the mPFC's ability to regulate BLA hyperactivity.
source: Further, the detrimental effects of stress will be compounded by the disruption of mPFC-BLA theta-frequency coherence and directional coupling, which is likely to impair the mPFC's ability to regulate BLA hyperactivity.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the current findings.

claim: Pre-conditioning stress has been shown to cause subsequent enhancement in fear learning that can last up to 90 days later.
source: Interestingly, pre-conditioning stress has been shown to cause subsequent enhancement in fear learning that can last up to 90 days later (Rau and Fanselow, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rau and Fanselow, 2009.

claim: Despite the effects of pre-conditioning stress on the encoding of fear memories, subsequent expression at later time points may no longer depend on BLA activity.
source: Our preliminary findings (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), taken together with the study by Do-Monte et al. (2015), suggest that despite the effects of pre-conditioning stress on the encoding of fear memories, subsequent expression at later time points may no longer depend on BLA activity.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the current findings and the Do-Monte et al. study.

claim: Other brain areas that interact with the BLA in the regulation of fear, such as the dmPFC, may play a role in maintaining expression of fear at remote time points.
source: This, in turn, raises the possibility that other brain areas that interact with the BLA in the regulation of fear, such as the dmPFC, may play a role in maintaining this expression at remote time points.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the current findings.

claim: The chronic immobilization stress paradigm used in the present study was previously shown to strengthen functional connectivity from the amygdala to the hippocampus.
source: Finally, it is interesting to note that the chronic immobilization stress paradigm used in the present study was previously shown to strengthen functional connectivity from the amygdala to the hippocampus (Ghosh et al., 2013), which undergoes stress-induced deficits similar to the mPFC (Arnsten, 2015; Chattarji et al., 2015; McEwen and Morrison, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ghosh et al., 2013; Arnsten, 2015; Chattarji et al., 2015; and McEwen and Morrison, 2013.

claim: The hippocampus undergoes stress-induced deficits similar to the mPFC.
source: Finally, it is interesting to note that the chronic immobilization stress paradigm used in the present study was previously shown to strengthen functional connectivity from the amygdala to the hippocampus (Ghosh et al., 2013), which undergoes stress-induced deficits similar to the mPFC (Arnsten, 2015; Chattarji et al., 2015; McEwen and Morrison, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arnsten, 2015; Chattarji et al., 2015; and McEwen and Morrison, 2013.

claim: Although both the hippocampus and mPFC undergo similar forms of stress-induced deficits, the impact of stress on their individual interactions with the amygdala are strikingly different.
source: In other words, although both the hippocampus and mPFC undergo similar forms of stress-induced deficits, the impact of stress on their individual interactions with the amygdala are strikingly different.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the current findings with previous literature.

claim: Naïve 8–9 weeks old male Sprague-Dawley rats weighing 300–350 grams were used in the study.
source: Naïve 8–9 weeks old male Sprague-Dawley rats (RRID: RGD_734476) weighing 300–350 grams at the start of the experiment (National Centre for Biological Sciences, Bangalore, India) and housed in groups of two were used in the study.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental subjects.

claim: All experiments were conducted in accordance with the guidelines of the CPCSEA, Government of India and approved by the Institutional Animal Ethics Committee of National Centre for Biological Sciences.
source: All experiments were conducted in accordance with the guidelines of the CPCSEA, Government of India and approved by the Institutional Animal Ethics Committee of National Centre for Biological Sciences.
evidence: This is a factual statement about ethical compliance.

claim: The animals in the CIS group were subjected to a 10 day chronic immobilization stress (CIS; 2 h/day for 10 consecutive days) from Day 2 to day 11.
